newsitem.title: USA: Exiles arrive at demonstration site off Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Exiles arrive at demonstration site off Cuba.

text.p: A flotilla of Cuban exile boats arrived on Saturday off Cuba's north coast to promote a national work stoppage on the Communist-ruled Caribbean island, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

The flotilla was the first of three scheduled for this year, leading up to Pope John Paul's visit to Cuba in early 1998. It arrived about 2:30 p.m EDT (1830 GMT) at Cuba's territorial 12-mile (19-km) limit, where a prayer service was to be held.
Cuba on Thursday described the flotilla as a "new attempt at a provocation" and said it would use "the necessary means" to ensure there were no violations of its territory.
Democracy Movement, the prominent Miami-based Cuban exile group that organised the flotilla, assured U.S. and Cuban authorities it did not intend to enter Cuban waters.

At least three dozen vessels headed toward the limit of Cuban territorial waters in two groups, organisers said. The first departed late on Friday and the second early on Saturday from locations in the Florida Keys.

The boats were to take up positions off Havana, Caibarien and the eastern tip of Cuba, and about a dozen aircraft were to join them. But a U.S. Coast Guard spokesman said bad weather in the Florida Straits, which separate Florida and Cuba, forced organisers to alter their plans.
"They ran into a little weather problem," Coast Guard Petty Officer Scott Carr said. "The planes aren't flying, and everybody else went to the Havana site."
No trouble was reported, Carr said. The Coast Guard said it was monitoring the flotilla but not escorting it.

Cuban exiles have taken a number of flotillas to the edge of Cuban territory in the Florida Straits. During a 1995 demonstration, a Democracy Movement boat entered Cuban territory and was sideswiped by Cuban military vessels.
In February 1996, Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two unarmed U.S. civilian planes between Florida and Cuba, killing four aviators for the exile group Brothers to the Rescue.

The incident provoked international outrage against Cuba. But President Fidel Castro's government defended its action by saying the planes were violating its territory. Washington said the downed planes were outside Cuban airspace and should not have been shot down.

Democracy Movement said Saturday's flotilla aimed to publicise within Cuba a general strike to be held at a time still to be determined. The group espouses nonviolent protest designed to bring about democratic reforms in Cuba.
Democracy Movement leaders have said they reserve their "right" as Cuban citizens to enter Cuban territory at any time and intend to exercise it during the pope's visit.
